Juvenile recruitment in Obliquaria reflexa begins with the release of glochidia that, following a brief parasitic phase, drop from the host fish and settle onto the substrate. At the moment of settlement, the prodissoconch shell length is approximately 0.03 centimeters , a minute size typical of unionid bivalves with an obligate parasitic larval stage. Newly metamorphosed juveniles emerge from the brooding adult at a shell length of 0.02 centimeters [Lb = 0.02 centimeters], measured at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], at an age of 10 days [ab = 10 days] since fertilisation. These initial dimensions are critical for understanding early life history constraints, as the tiny spat must immediately begin filter-feeding to support rapid shell growth. The transition from parasitic larva to free-living juvenile represents a major demographic bottleneck, with high mortality expected during the first weeks post-settlement due to predation and inadequate food availability. Laboratory rearing experiments have confirmed that these values are consistent across multiple cohorts when temperature is controlled, providing a reliable baseline for modeling early growth trajectories in this species.

The ultimate shell length attained by Obliquaria reflexa has been recorded at 5.3 centimeters [Li = 5.3 centimeters], representing the asymptotic size achieved under favorable environmental conditions in the wild. This maximum dimension was documented from long-term mark-recapture studies conducted in the Mobile River basin, where individuals were followed over multiple decades. Consistent with this shell size, the ultimate dry weight of the soft tissues reaches 5.4 grams [Wwi = 5.4 grams], a value derived from size-corrected allometric relationships observed in related unionid taxa. This dry mass is substantially lower than that of sympatric species such as Elliptio crassidens, reflecting differences in shell thickness and tissue density. The attainment of asymptotic size appears to be governed largely by resource availability, as individuals from nutritionally poor headwater streams rarely approach the maximum shell length seen in larger river channels. Shell growth increments slow markedly after approximately 15 years, with most linear gain concentrated in the first decade of life.

Reproductive output in Obliquaria reflexa is expressed through the production of glochidia by gravid females. At a shell length of 4.88 centimeters, which corresponds to a moderately large adult, the daily reproduction rate can be inferred from the total annual fecundity and spawning frequency. Field surveys indicate that females produce approximately 112 glochidia per day [Ri = approximately 112 glochidia per day] when water temperatures are held at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a rate sustained over the course of the spring spawning period. This daily production translates to roughly 41,000 glochidia released over a single reproductive season, a fecundity that is intermediate among North American unionids. The timing of glochidial release is tightly linked to thermal cues, with peak spawning activity coinciding with the warm-water period following the spring equinox. Such high fecundity is necessary to compensate for the low probability of encountering a suitable host fish and the subsequent mortality of the parasitic larvae before metamorphosis.

A major life history transition occurs when Obliquaria reflexa attains puberty, defined as the shell length at which individuals first develop functional gonads and become capable of spawning. Based on growth trajectory data and the known age at sexual maturity of approximately two decades, the shell length at puberty has been determined to be 2.5 centimeters [Lp = 2.5 centimeters]. This relatively large size at maturation reflects the slow growth rate characteristic of long-lived freshwater mussels, which prioritize structural investment over early reproduction. Individuals below this threshold allocate energy exclusively to somatic growth and shell deposition, only shifting resources toward gametogenesis once they have surpassed the 2.5 centimeter mark. The late onset of reproductive activity is a common life history strategy among unionids inhabiting stable, low-disturbance environments, where adult survival is high and the benefits of delayed reproduction outweigh the costs. This pattern contrasts sharply with short-lived species that mature at much smaller sizes and produce fewer offspring per reproductive event.

The lifespan of Obliquaria reflexa has been estimated at approximately 23 years [am = approximately 23 years] under natural conditions, based on shell annuli counts and mark-recapture data collected at a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. This extended longevity is typical of many freshwater mussel species and is accompanied by a gradual decline in reproductive output in the oldest age classes. Annual survivorship remains high through the first two decades, with natural mortality primarily attributed to senescence in the last few years of life. The combination of a 23-year lifespan (23 years) [am = 23 years], delayed maturation at 2.5 centimeters shell length, and the production of approximately 112 glochidia per day throughout the reproductive window creates a life history that emphasizes iteroparity and bet-hedging over a single, high-investment reproductive event at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Individuals in the wild have been documented to live past 25 years, but the 23-year figure represents the most robust central estimate from long-term demography studies in the Tombigbee River system. Comparative data from other unionids suggest that this lifespan is conserved within the genus.
